case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a public body answering a FOIA request must segregate or redact exempt material and disclose the rest, so the City had to produce redacted records even though the requester had not initially asked for redacted material, and it prescribed the Vaughn index and affidavit a body must supply when it withholds.
key_cases.relevance: It is the practical tool by which oversight bodies and citizens force production of agency records.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the City was required to provide Mr. Farley this redacted material in response to his original FOIA request

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that States make 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families does not create a right enforceable by beneficiaries through § 1983 or an implied right of action.
key_cases.relevance: Enforcement of federal child-welfare standards runs through federal administrative oversight, not private suits.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of Carlita B.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming termination of parental rights, the Court held the improvement periods and family case plans afforded the mother were more than adequate, and directed that abuse and neglect cases be given the highest priority with systems developed to monitor their progress and prevent delay.
key_cases.relevance: The Court ordered the Administrative Director to build systems monitoring the status and progress of abuse and neglect cases, the state-court analogue of systemic oversight triggers.
key_cases.quote: Unjustified procedural delays wreak havoc on a child's development, stability and security.

key_cases.case_name: Daily Gazette Co. v. West Virginia Development Office
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Remanding with directions, the Court held that a public body withholding records under the internal-memoranda exemption must produce a Vaughn index justifying each document and a supporting affidavit, and that the exemption covers only deliberative advice, opinions and recommendations, not ordinary communications with private parties.
key_cases.relevance: Oversight of an agency begins with its records, and this decision sets out precisely what the agency must establish, document by document, before it may withhold them.
key_cases.quote: The Vaughn index must provide a relatively detailed justification as to why each document is exempt, specifically identifying the reasons why W. Va.Code, 29B-1-4(8) [1977] is relevant

reporting_details: Mandated reporters listed in W. Va. Code § 49-2-803(a) must report immediately, and not more than 24 hours after suspecting the abuse or neglect, to the Department of Human Services; reporting is not universal — any other person may report but is not required to (§ 49-2-803(c)). Reports go to one statewide centralized intake maintained by the Bureau for Social Services, reachable by a 24-hour, seven-day-a-week hotline (1-800-352-6513, option 2) or by web-based reporting (email, electronic fax, fillable form, or other electronic form) that sends the report to a live person to handle it immediately; both systems give the reporter a specific case identifier immediately upon making a report (§ 49-2-809(a)). In any case where the reporter believes the child suffered serious physical abuse or sexual abuse or sexual assault, the reporter shall also immediately report to the State Police and any law-enforcement agency having jurisdiction to investigate the complaint (§ 49-2-803(a)). Knowingly failing to report is a misdemeanor punishable by confinement in jail not more than 90 days or a fine of not more than $5,000 (§ 49-2-812(a)); where the child is known or suspected to be sexually assaulted or sexually abused, or a student is known or suspected to have been the victim of non-consensual sexual contact, sexual intercourse, or sexual intrusion on school premises, the penalty is not more than six months or not more than $10,000 (§ 49-2-812(b)).
